psoas_minor.noteTxt: Psoas minor — no mesh on this page. NO PAGE SHIPS IT, and no source this project holds contains it. Verified three ways: (1) all six pages' own structure lists contain no psoas minor -- only Iliopsoas / Iliopsoas tendon on the two Imaging pages and Psoas major / Iliacus / Iliopsoas fascia / Iliopsoas bursa on the four Z pages; (2) the pinned upstream Z-Anatomy catalogue (data/derived/zanatomy_inventory.json, commit 6c7f9016) has 3,572 named objects and none of them is a psoas minor; (3) the string does not occur anywhere in this repository. This is also the EXPECTED finding: the psoas minor is absent in a large share of people. Raja 2026 (Cureus 18(6):e111450, doi:10.7759/cureus.111450): "The psoas minor is a slender, inconstantly present vestigial muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. Classical texts report its presence in 40-50% of individuals" -- and in their own 30 cadavers it was found in 2 (6.67%; 3 of 60 sides, 5.00%), arising from the bodies of T12 and L1 and inserting by a long slender tendon into the pecten pubis and the iliopubic eminence (belly 4.57 +/- 0.46 cm, tendon 17.17 +/- 0.85 cm, total 21.73 +/- 0.45 cm). So its absence on these two bodies is a real anatomical possibility and not a segmentation failure -- but nothing here can prove it for THIS body either, because neither CT was read for it. Before Q306 the four Z pages answered this query with Psoas major at rank 1 and no note at all, which is a wrong answer rather than an honest absence. This project's name for it: Psoas minor (musculus psoas minor). It offers 10 structures this page does carry.

lateral pelvic tilt.line: Lateral pelvic tilt (pelvic obliquity) הטיית אגן צידית a concept, not a structureOne side of the pelvis drops relative to the other in the frontal plane. In single-leg stance the STANCE-side hip abductors hold the pelvis level; when they fail, the opposite (swing) side drops. The quadratus lumborum acts on the pelvis from above.3 cited sourcesWeaker hip abductors go with a greater drop of the opposite side of the pelvis: runners who developed medial tibial stress syndrome had "weaker hip abductors (P = 0.008)" and "greater contralateral pelvic drop (P = 0.021)". Becker J, Nakajima M, Wu WFW. Factors Contributing to Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome in Runners: A Prospective Study. Pick one of the three below to see the muscles that produce it on this page.The three tilts are the standard clinical description; each has its own entry with its own sources.Mark the 4 structuresAnterolateral abdominal wallErector spinaeGluteal group (superficial)HamstringsFlexion at the hip jointExtension at the hip jointAbduction at the hip jointFlexion at the lumbar spineLateral flexion (side bending) at the lumbar spineAnterior pelvic tilt הטיית אגן קדמית a concept, not a structureThe pelvis rotates forward about the hip joints, so the ASIS moves below the PSIS and lumbar lordosis tends to increase. Produced / maintained by the HIP FLEXORS in front and the lumbar extensors behind.3 cited sourcesStretching the hip flexors reduced anterior pelvic tilt: "a mean increase of 2.6 deg in passive hip extension and a corresponding mean reduction of 1.2 deg in anterior pelvic tilt" (P < .001). Preece SJ, Tan YF, Alghamdi TDA, Arnall FA. Comparison of Pelvic Tilt Before and After Hip Flexor Stretching in Healthy Adults. J Manipulative Physiol Ther 2021;44(4):289-294. doi:10.1016/j.jmpt.2020.09.006 (PMID 34090549)The lumbar multifidus is more active in anterior than in posterior pelvic tilt: "MF muscle activity during the exercise involving PPT was significantly lower than that involving APT". Jang TJ, Jeon IC. Effects of pelvic tilt control using visual biofeedback on gluteus maximus, multifidus, and hamstring activities during three different bridge exercises. Physiother Theory Pract 2024;40(12):2795-2804. doi:10.1080/09593985.2023.2297001 (PMID 38329074)The hip flexor group named by this project's own cited action data is the iliopsoas (psoas major and iliacus), rectus femoris, sartorius and adductor longus. Produced by the HIP EXTENSORS (gluteus maximus, hamstrings) and the ABDOMINAL WALL.3 cited sourcesGluteus maximus is more active in posterior pelvic tilt than in anterior or neutral: "GM muscle activity during the exercise involving PPT was significantly higher than that involving APT and NPT". In single-leg stance the STANCE-side hip abductors hold the pelvis level; when they fail, the opposite (swing) side drops. The quadratus lumborum acts on the pelvis from above.3 cited sourcesWeaker hip abductors go with a greater drop of the opposite side of the pelvis: runners who developed medial tibial stress syndrome had "weaker hip abductors (P = 0.008)" and "greater contralateral pelvic drop (P = 0.021)". הטיית אגן.noteTxt: Psoas minor — no mesh on this page. NO PAGE SHIPS IT, and no source this project holds contains it. Verified three ways: (1) all six pages' own structure lists contain no psoas minor -- only Iliopsoas / Iliopsoas tendon on the two Imaging pages and Psoas major / Iliacus / Iliopsoas fascia / Iliopsoas bursa on the four Z pages; (2) the pinned upstream Z-Anatomy catalogue (data/derived/zanatomy_inventory.json, commit 6c7f9016) has 3,572 named objects and none of them is a psoas minor; (3) the string does not occur anywhere in this repository. This is also the EXPECTED finding: the psoas minor is absent in a large share of people. Raja 2026 (Cureus 18(6):e111450, doi:10.7759/cureus.111450): "The psoas minor is a slender, inconstantly present vestigial muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. Classical texts report its presence in 40-50% of individuals" -- and in their own 30 cadavers it was found in 2 (6.67%; 3 of 60 sides, 5.00%), arising from the bodies of T12 and L1 and inserting by a long slender tendon into the pecten pubis and the iliopubic eminence (belly 4.57 +/- 0.46 cm, tendon 17.17 +/- 0.85 cm, total 21.73 +/- 0.45 cm). Patra 2024 (Folia Morphol 83(4):886-892, doi:10.5603/fm.99128) calls it "the most unstable muscle of the psoas group", found it in 12 of 30 cadavers, and notes that "the muscle's distal attachment to the iliac fascia may partially control the position and mechanical stability of the underlying iliopsoas". So its absence on these two bodies is a real anatomical possibility and not a segmentation failure -- but nothing here can prove it for THIS body either, because neither CT was read for it. Before Q306 the four Z pages answered this query with Psoas major at rank 1 and no note at all, which is a wrong answer rather than an honest absence. This project's name for it: Psoas minor (musculus psoas minor). It offers 7 structures this page does carry.
